strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: knowledge distillation when the student training set contains unknown spurious correlations or entirely missing groups. The framing is clear and relevant to robust vision deployment.

The proposed ConfiG method is simple and well motivated: use a robust teacher and a biased auxiliary student to guide diffusion edits toward samples where the teacher remains confident but the student is not. This directly targets the failure mode rather than only increasing generic data diversity.

Empirical gains on the controlled group-shift settings are substantial, especially for worst-group accuracy. On CelebA, ConfiG with CutMix and EDRM improves worst-group accuracy from 38.9% for CutMix alone and 54.0% for ActGen to 66.1%, nearly matching the teacher. On SpuCo Birds, it improves worst-group accuracy from 52.7% for ActGen/DAFusion to 62.7%.

The experimental section includes several useful comparisons and ablations: ERM vs EDRM, standard augmentations, multiple diffusion augmentation baselines, different student architectures, larger CelebA training data, number of synthetic augmentations, and cost-vs-quality analysis.

The qualitative examples support the intended behavior of the method: ConfiG appears to change spurious attributes while often preserving the causal class attribute better than the compared diffusion augmentation methods.

The limitations section is unusually candid about the need for a robust teacher, including the fact that the SpuCo Birds teacher had to be trained with access to balanced data that would not be available in the intended practical setting.
weaknesses: The theoretical result in Appendix A.1 appears mathematically problematic. In Proposition 1, the condition alpha <= Omega/(2Theta) does not imply |Omega_aug| <= Omega/2; it would instead make the improvement at most alpha Theta and can leave Omega_aug close to Omega for small alpha. The bound |Omega_aug| <= min{Omega - Theta, Omega/2} also seems to ignore the factor alpha. This weakens the claimed theoretical support.

The strongest results rely on artificially constructed covariate shifts where the missing groups and spurious attributes are known to the experimenter. This is useful for controlled evaluation, but it only partially validates the claim of robustness to unknown real-world covariate shift.

The method depends critically on a teacher that is already robust on the missing or shifted groups. This is a strong assumption. The SpuCo Birds experiment in particular uses a ViT-B teacher fine-tuned on a balanced dataset containing the otherwise missing groups, which undercuts the practicality of that result despite being acknowledged.

The improvement on Spurious ImageNet is quite small: ConfiG improves mAUC over ActGen by about 0.5 points and validation accuracy is not consistently best. This makes the evidence for scalability to less controlled, class-level spurious features weaker than the group-shift results.

The method is computationally expensive because each generated image requires null-text inversion and several optimization steps through the diffusion decoder. The paper reports 11.4 seconds per image on a V100, which may limit practical use for larger datasets.

The comparison to baselines may not fully isolate the contribution of teacher-student disagreement guidance from other implementation choices. For example, ConfiG uses explicit teacher confidence during generation while many baselines are not designed for this KD setting; stronger adaptations of baselines to use the same teacher signal would make the comparison more conclusive.

The generated augmentations are assumed to preserve the correct label when the teacher confidence is high, but teacher confidence is not a guarantee of semantic or label correctness, especially under distribution shift. More quantitative filtering or human/automatic validation of generated image correctness would strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility is reasonable in terms of hyperparameters and prompts, but the paper does not clearly state whether code, generated datasets, or exact splits will be released. Given the cost and sensitivity of diffusion-guided generation, this matters for independent verification.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: knowledge distillation under covariate shift when the missing or spurious groups are not annotated. This is an important practical setting for deploying smaller vision models distilled from stronger foundation models.

The core idea is intuitive and plausible: use teacher-student disagreement, with high teacher confidence and low student confidence, to guide diffusion-based augmentations toward samples that expose shortcuts learned by the student.

The empirical results on the constructed CelebA and SpuCo Birds settings show clear improvements in worst-group accuracy over several diffusion augmentation baselines, and the authors include ablations over augmentation count, student architecture, stronger conventional augmentations, larger CelebA training size, and combination with TAB.
The paper is generally readable and includes useful implementation details, computational cost discussion, and an explicit limitation acknowledging dependence on a robust teacher.
weaknesses: The main experimental settings are highly controlled and somewhat artificial. CelebA and SpuCo Birds are manually subsampled to remove particular groups, and the method is evaluated largely on these designed shifts. This weakens the claim that ConfiG handles unknown covariate shift in realistic deployment scenarios.

The method relies critically on access to a teacher that is robust on the missing test groups. For SpuCo Birds, the authors explicitly state that CLIP was not sufficiently robust and instead fine-tune a ViT-B using a balanced training set. This substantially undercuts the practical premise: if balanced data is needed to obtain the teacher, the setting is no longer fully aligned with unknown missing groups.

The theoretical analysis is not convincing. The proposition assumes augmentations already come from a set with high teacher confidence and low student confidence, which is close to the desired conclusion. More seriously, the proof appears to contain algebraic inconsistencies: from Omega_aug <= Omega - alpha Theta with alpha <= min{1, Omega/(2Theta)}, it does not follow that |Omega_aug| <= min{Omega - Theta, Omega/2}; the stated bound would require different conditions on alpha and also needs a lower bound to control the absolute value. This makes the claimed theoretical guarantee unreliable.

The novelty is incremental relative to guided diffusion, classifier-disagreement/counterfactual generation, and ActGen-style active generation. The paper’s contribution is a reasonable adaptation to KD, but the algorithmic step is fairly direct: optimize a latent image so the teacher remains confident while the student becomes unconfident.

The ImageNet evidence is weak. On Spurious ImageNet, the reported gains are very small, e.g. around 0.5 mAUC over ActGen, with no standard deviations or statistical analysis. This makes it hard to judge whether the method meaningfully improves robustness beyond the toy/group-subset settings.

The evaluation does not sufficiently verify the semantic correctness of generated samples. The method assumes teacher confidence preserves the causal label, but diffusion edits can alter class-relevant attributes or introduce artifacts. Qualitative examples are limited, and there is no systematic human or automated audit of label preservation and visual quality.

The comparison to baselines may still be confounded by teacher usage and optimization cost. ConfiG uses both teacher and student signals and is substantially more expensive per image than several baselines; while the appendix discusses cost-vs-quality, the fairness of comparing methods under fixed augmentation count rather than fixed compute remains only partially addressed.

The paper’s claims are broader than the evidence supports. The results show promise under a strong-teacher assumption and curated covariate shifts, but they do not convincingly establish a general solution for unknown covariate shift in knowledge distillation. Given the dependence on a robust teacher, limited real-world validation, small ImageNet gains, and flawed theory, I would not support acceptance in its current form.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: knowledge distillation when the available training data contains unknown spurious correlations and missing groups. The motivation is clear, and the setting is highly relevant for deploying compact vision models distilled from stronger foundation models.

The proposed ConfiG method is simple and well aligned with the problem: use teacher-student confidence disagreement to guide diffusion-based augmentations toward samples that preserve teacher confidence while reducing student confidence. This is a plausible and original way to expose shortcuts learned by the student without requiring group annotations.

The empirical evidence is strong on the main controlled group-shift benchmarks. On CelebA and SpuCo Birds, ConfiG consistently improves group mean and especially worst-group accuracy over ERM, EDRM, stronger standard augmentations, and several diffusion-augmentation baselines. The gains over ActGen in worst-group accuracy are particularly meaningful.

The paper includes useful ablations: number of synthetic augmentations, combination with TAB, different student architectures, larger training sets, ERM vs EDRM, and cost-quality comparisons. These make the empirical case more convincing than a single-table result.

The qualitative examples and the analysis of student loss/accuracy on generated augmentations support the intended mechanism: ConfiG appears to produce harder, more shortcut-breaking samples than the baselines while retaining the teacher's target class.
The limitations section is unusually candid, especially about the need for a robust teacher and the impracticality of the fine-tuned SpuCo Birds teacher in a fully realistic deployment scenario.
weaknesses: The method relies heavily on the availability of a teacher that is robust on the absent or shifted groups. This is not a minor assumption: in SpuCo Birds, the intended CLIP teacher is reported to have poor worst-group performance, so the authors fine-tune a ViT-B on a balanced dataset that would not be available in the motivating unknown-shift setting. This limits the practical generality of the strongest results.

The theoretical analysis is not fully convincing. The final bound appears to have inconsistencies: the proposition states a condition involving δt + 2δs, while the proof derives a denominator with δt + δs; more importantly, the step from Ωaug ≤ Ω − αΘ to |Ωaug| ≤ min{Ω − Θ, Ω/2} does not follow under the stated condition α ≤ Ω/(2Θ). This weakens the claimed theoretical support, though the empirical contribution remains valuable.

The experimental setting is partly synthetic/constructed: CelebA and SpuCo Birds splits deliberately remove known attribute groups, while the method is framed as handling unknown spurious features. This is a reasonable evaluation protocol, but the paper would be stronger with more naturally occurring unknown shifts or a setting where neither the authors nor the teacher construction uses privileged group knowledge.

The ImageNet evidence is positive but modest. ConfiG improves spurious mAUC over baselines, but the margins are small, and the validation accuracy differences are mixed. This supports broader applicability but less decisively than the group-shift experiments.

Computational cost is substantial: ConfiG requires null-text inversion and iterative latent optimization with teacher and student evaluations, reported at 11.4 seconds per image on a V100. The paper argues quality outweighs quantity, but the cost may be prohibitive for larger-scale augmentation pipelines.

Reproducibility would benefit from more implementation detail about baseline tuning, diffusion prompts, random seeds, and exact data split construction. The paper reports many useful hyperparameters, but the fairness of comparing several diffusion-augmentation baselines can be sensitive to such details.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: knowledge distillation under covariate shift when the limited training set omits relevant groups. The framing around teacher-student disagreement is intuitive and appropriate for unknown spurious correlations.

ConfiG is a technically plausible and reasonably original method that uses a robust teacher, a biased auxiliary student, and diffusion latent optimization to generate samples that are difficult for the student while remaining high-confidence for the teacher.

The empirical evidence is strong overall. The method is evaluated on CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, and ImageNet-100/Spurious ImageNet, with comparisons to several recent diffusion augmentation baselines. The gains in worst-group accuracy are especially convincing on CelebA-HQ and SpuCo Birds, and ImageNet-100 results suggest the approach is not limited to hand-constructed group benchmarks.

The ablations are useful: the paper separates inter-class mixing from latent optimization, tests stronger standard augmentations, more synthetic samples, weaker teachers, different replacement probabilities, other architectures, and combinations with model-centric debiasing methods.
The manuscript is generally clear and reproducible. It provides training details, generation hyperparameters, compute estimates, baseline descriptions, qualitative examples, and failure cases.
weaknesses: The approach depends heavily on a strong and well-calibrated teacher and a capable generative model. This is acknowledged, but it limits the generality of the method and makes the headline claim of handling unknown covariate shift conditional on substantial external prior knowledge encoded in CLIP/BEiT and Stable Diffusion.

The experimental shifts are partly synthetic or curated: groups are deliberately removed from CelebA-HQ and SpuCo Birds, BAR is a specific biased benchmark, and ImageNet-100 is selected using Spurious ImageNet components. This is reasonable for evaluation, but the evidence for real-world unknown covariate shift remains limited.

The method is computationally expensive and operationally complex, involving null-text inversion, prompt-to-prompt editing, latent optimization, foreground regularization, teacher and auxiliary student inference, and filtering/stopping heuristics. The FLOP-matched comparison is helpful, but excludes some one-time costs and may not fully capture wall-clock or engineering overhead.

The theoretical section is mainly motivational. It analyzes conditions under which augmentations reduce a fixed risk gap, but the assumptions are strong and hard to verify, and it does not directly characterize the retrained student produced by the full algorithm.

Some results are less decisive than the strongest claims suggest. On BAR in the main table, ConfiG is second-best and only slightly below Diff-Mix; with larger SpuCo training data the gap to baselines narrows; and ImageNet-100 appears to be run once due to cost, so variance is unknown.

There is limited discussion of potential societal issues despite using binary gender classification on face images and synthetic face manipulation. This does not invalidate the technical contribution, but a stronger treatment would be appropriate for this application context.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: knowledge distillation when limited training data induces covariate shift and shortcut learning. This is a meaningful setting for compact vision models, and the paper’s focus on worst-group behavior is appropriate.

The proposed ConfiG pipeline is technically coherent: it uses teacher-student disagreement to guide diffusion-based augmentations, combines inter-class editing with latent optimization, and gives a reasonable empirical motivation that disagreements concentrate on missing groups.

The experimental section is broader than many augmentation papers: CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, and ImageNet-100 are considered, with comparisons to several recent diffusion augmentation baselines, stronger standard augmentations, weaker teachers, different architectures, replacement probabilities, and more augmentations.

The main results show consistent improvements in group-robust metrics, especially WGA/GMA on CelebA-HQ and SpuCo Birds. The ablations also support the claim that inter-class mixing plus disagreement optimization is stronger than either component alone.
The paper is generally clear and includes useful implementation details, compute accounting, qualitative examples, and an honest discussion of some failure cases and limitations.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental. ConfiG appears to be a combination of existing diffusion inversion/editing machinery, inter-class diffusion mixup, and adversarial/active generation using model confidence. The paper demonstrates this combination well, but the conceptual leap over ActGen, Diff-Mix, and DiG-IN is moderate.

The experimental setting is quite tailored to the method. Several main datasets use manually constructed or highly restricted covariate-shift splits with groups fully absent from training, and the method assumes a robust teacher that already handles the missing groups. This limits how strongly the results establish usefulness under naturally occurring unknown shift.

The fairness of the compute-matched comparison is not fully convincing. The paper excludes some one-time preprocessing costs and estimates ConfiG backward-pass costs by a fixed multiplier; since ConfiG is expensive and optimization-heavy, small accounting choices could affect how many baseline samples are allowed.

Some empirical claims are weaker than the headline suggests. On BAR, ConfiG is second to Diff-Mix in the main table; with stronger standard augmentations, real-data baselines already improve substantially; with a larger SpuCo training set, the gain over Diff-Mix is within standard deviation; and without covariate shift, ConfiG is poor unless heavily scaled.

ImageNet-100 results are reported without repeated runs, despite being used to support generality beyond group-shift benchmarks. The improvements there are modest, so variance estimates would be important.

The theoretical analysis is mostly motivational rather than probative. Its assumptions effectively require a well-calibrated teacher, label-preserving augmentations, and a distribution Q that is more challenging for the student than the teacher; these are close to the desired outcome and are not verifiable in practice.

Label preservation is not fully resolved. The method relies on high teacher confidence to preserve class semantics, but qualitative failure cases show out-of-distribution or semantically questionable generations, especially for harder classes such as BAR. More systematic filtering or human/independent validation would strengthen the case.

The method’s dependence on strong foundation teachers and diffusion models narrows its practical appeal. It may be most useful precisely when large robust models and expensive generation are already available, and the paper does not sufficiently quantify end-to-end cost versus simpler robust-training or data-collection alternatives.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated Algorithms/General problem: knowledge distillation when limited training data misses groups or covariates that appear at test time. The teacher-student disagreement framing is intuitive and well aligned with the stated covariate-shift setting.

The proposed ConfiG method is technically clear: it combines inter-class diffusion editing with latent optimization to preserve teacher confidence while lowering student confidence, producing targeted hard augmentations without requiring group annotations or explicit knowledge of the spurious feature.

The empirical evidence is strong overall. Results cover CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, and ImageNet-100, with comparisons to several recent diffusion-based augmentation baselines. ConfiG consistently improves worst-group and group-mean accuracy in the group-shift settings and improves validation accuracy and SpuScore on ImageNet-100.

The paper includes useful ablations: inter-class mixing versus latent optimization, stronger standard augmentations, more synthetic samples, weaker teachers, different architectures, replacement probability, and larger SpuCo Birds training data. These make the empirical story more convincing than a single benchmark table.

The authors make a reasonable effort at fair comparison by approximately matching augmentation generation FLOPs and documenting hyperparameters, dataset construction, prompts, and training details. The qualitative examples and failure-case analysis also help interpret what the method is doing.

The limitations are stated honestly: the method is classification-focused, depends on pretrained teacher and diffusion models, can fail when generation is poor or optimization stalls, and is computationally expensive.
weaknesses: The method depends heavily on access to a strong and well-calibrated teacher whose decision boundary is reliable on both training and shifted test regions. This is central to the method and theory, but in many practical covariate-shift settings the teacher may share similar biases or be unreliable on the missing groups.

The computational cost is substantial. ConfiG requires inversion, inter-class editing, backpropagation through the diffusion pipeline, an auxiliary student, and teacher/student evaluations. Although the paper compares FLOPs, the practical wall-clock and engineering burden may limit adoption.

The main covariate-shift settings are somewhat controlled or constructed, especially CelebA-HQ and SpuCo Birds with deliberately removed groups. The ImageNet-100 setting is broader but appears to use one training run, so statistical reliability there is weaker.

Some gains are not uniformly decisive. On BAR, ConfiG is second-best in the main table and stronger conventional augmentations close much of the gap. With a larger SpuCo Birds train set containing bias-conflicting samples, the improvement over Diff-Mix is within standard deviation. Without covariate shift, ConfiG is initially much worse than Diff-Mix and ActGen unless scaled to many augmentations.

The theoretical analysis is mostly motivational. Its assumptions, including bounded teacher KL over generated samples, sufficiently large teacher-student confidence gaps, and favorable augmented distribution support, are hard to verify and do not provide a practical criterion for choosing alpha or validating Q.

The fairness of baseline comparisons is plausible but not airtight: ConfiG is optimized specifically for teacher-student disagreement in a distillation setting, while several baselines are generic augmentation methods. More discussion of baseline tuning under this exact objective would strengthen the claim of superiority.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed appendices, but the manuscript does not clearly state code or generated-data release plans. Given the complexity of DiG-IN, null-text inversion, prompt choices, FLOP accounting, and baseline implementations, this matters.
